newsitem.title: USA: Lockheed, Northrop to merge in $11.6 billion deal.
newsitem.headline: Lockheed, Northrop to merge in $11.6 billion deal.

text.p: Aerospace goliaths Lockheed Martin Corp. and Northrop Grumman Corp. plan to merge in a deal valued at $11.6 billion, the companies said on Thursday.
In a joint press release, they said Northrop shareholders would receive 1.1923 shares of Lockheed for each share of Northrop.

The deal will create a company with annual revenues of $37 billion and a global workforce of about 230,000 employees. The transaction is expected to close by year-end, pending shareholder and regulatory approvals, the companies said.
Leaders of the two companies said the combination was needed to bolster their positions in an increasingly competitive worldwide marketplace.

"Lockheed Martin and Northrop Grumman have been leaders in consolidating the aerospace industry, and we are now taking the next logical step in combining together to shape the future," Lockheed Chairman and Chief Executive Officer Norman Augustine said.

The companies said they hoped to account for the merger as a pooling of interests but might be forced to account for it as a purchase. The effect of the merger will be neutral on 1998 earnings but will be increasingly accretive thereafter, they said.
A definitive merger agreement has been approved unanimously by the boards of directors of both companies.
Northrop Chairman, President and CEO Kent Kresa will become vice chairman of Lockheed, and two other Northrop board members also will join the Lockheed board.
Kresa will "have a strong role in the transition," the companies said
The companies have cooperated in the past on such U.S. Defense Department contracts as the Joint Strike Fighter, the F-22, and airborne early warning systems.

The companies said the merger will expand critical mass in electronics, military aircraft, commercial aerostructures and information systems; increase breadth and depth in composites, data processing, stealth, sensors, microelectronics and manufacturing; and enhance systems engineering and platform integration capabilities.
Lockheed, based in Bethesda, Md., employs 180,000 people and had 1996 sales of $27 billion. Los Angeles-based Northrop employes 45,000 and had 1996 revenues of $8 billion.
Lockheed has retained Bear, Stearns & Co Inc. and Lehman Brothers Inc. as its financial advisers in the deal. Northrop is being advised by Salomon Brothers.
